balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Ford Motor Company: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings, which for Ford is almost entirely Ford Credit's funding debt -- consolidated TotalDebt is roughly $160bn, of which Ford Credit alone carries ~$135-141bn against its own receivables; Automotive (industrial) debt is only ~$20-24bn.

For Ford Motor Company: do not read consolidated debt as industrial leverage. The DCF's net-debt bridge uses Automotive Debt (the KPI card above) netted against Company cash, and values Ford Credit separately at ~1.0x book equity since its debt is matched by finance receivables, not a claim on the industrial business's cash flow.

What to watch:

  • Automotive debt trend versus industrial EBITDA, not consolidated figures
  • Ford Credit's leverage ratio (debt/equity, disclosed in filings as ~9-10:1) and loss-to-receivables trend, which drive how much equity it actually needs

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Ford Motor Company: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Ford Motor Company: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Ford Motor Company: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Ford Motor Company: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Ford Motor Company: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Ford Motor Company: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Ford Motor Company: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentEbit.title: Segment EBIT
segmentEbit.content:
Ford reports four operating segments: Ford Blue (gas and hybrid vehicles), Ford Model e (EVs), Ford Pro (commercial and government fleet, including software/service attachments) and Ford Credit (captive auto finance). Each discloses its own EBIT.

For Ford: this is the central tension in the investment case. Ford Blue and Ford Pro have together generated roughly $10-16bn of annual EBIT, while Ford Model e has lost $2-5bn a year since the segment was broken out in FY2022 funding the EV transition. Ford Credit's EBIT reflects its own leveraged balance sheet (receivables funded by debt), not the industrial business, and the DCF values it separately at book equity rather than including its earnings in the owner-FCF stream.

What to watch:

  • Whether Model e's losses are narrowing (management has guided toward break-even) or still widening
  • Ford Pro's EBIT margin, which has been the strongest of the three industrial segments on fleet/software attach
  • Ford Blue funding Model e: if Blue's EBIT falls while Model e's losses persist, consolidated cash generation compresses from both sides

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
Revenue by the same three industrial segments (Ford Credit's revenue is financing income on receivables, not shown here to keep the scale comparable).

For Ford: Model e revenue is small and volatile relative to Blue and Pro -- a few billion dollars against Blue's ~$100bn and Pro's ~$60-67bn -- so its EBIT losses are a profitability problem, not a scale problem. Pro has grown revenue every year since the 2023 segment split; Blue's is roughly flat.

What to watch:

  • Pro's revenue growth continuing (fleet electrification and software/service attach are the stated drivers)
  • Model e revenue growth outpacing its losses, i.e. the loss per vehicle narrowing

wholesales.title: Wholesale unit volumes
wholesales.content:
Wholesales are vehicles shipped to dealers (the revenue-recognition point), broken out by segment, in thousands of units.

For Ford: volume and mix both matter here -- Model e's unit volumes are a small fraction of Blue's (roughly 100-180k vs. ~2.7-2.9m a year) even though EV capex has been sized for a much larger ramp, which is the crux of the overcapacity/mix argument. Pro's unit volumes have grown alongside its revenue and EBIT.

What to watch:

  • Model e wholesale growth (or lack of it) against the capex already committed
  • Revenue per unit by segment (Pro's software/service attach should lift this over the raw wholesale count)

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Ford Motor Company: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
